mcqs.question: Why is a process's code (text) segment typically marked read-only and executable, but not writable?
options: So that shared library code pages compress better on disk
To prevent a bug or exploit from modifying the program's own instructions at runtime
Because the compiler cannot produce writable machine code
mcqs.explanation: Marking code read+execute but not writable stops accidental or malicious modification of instructions in memory — a key defense against certain exploit techniques. It isn't about saving space or disk compression, and compilers can absolutely emit writable code; the restriction is a deliberate protection choice.

mcqs.question: Two processes both link the same shared library. Under segmentation, how can they share its code without sharing their private data?
options: Each process's segment table has a code-segment entry pointing at the same physical base, while their data and stack segment entries point elsewhere
The OS copies the library's code into each process's memory separately
Sharing under segmentation requires both processes to use identical stack segments too
This isn't possible under segmentation, only under paging
mcqs.explanation: Segmentation makes sharing a matter of pointing one segment table entry at shared physical memory, while other entries (data, stack) stay private per process. It doesn't require copying the code per process, doesn't force shared stacks, and is very much possible under segmentation.

mcqs.question: In segmentation-with-paging, what does a segment table entry point to, instead of a raw physical base address?
options: A page table for that segment, so the segment's pages can be scattered across non-contiguous physical frames
A second segment table for redundancy
A fixed list of physical addresses computed at compile time
Nothing — segmentation-with-paging removes segment tables entirely
mcqs.explanation: Each segment gets its own page table, letting that segment's contents live in any free frames rather than needing one contiguous physical range — this is exactly what removes external fragmentation while keeping segments as logical units. There's no redundant second table, no compile-time address list, and segment tables are very much still present.

mcqs.question: What's the sharper way to distinguish segmentation from paging, beyond "variable size vs fixed size"?
options: Segmentation gives the programmer's logical view of memory hardware representation (for protection and sharing); paging is purely a physical placement mechanism unaware of what a page contains
Segmentation is strictly faster than paging at address translation
Paging cannot support any form of memory protection
Segmentation is only used in embedded systems today
mcqs.explanation: The deeper distinction is purpose: segmentation encodes logical structure and protection boundaries meaningful to the program, while paging solves physical placement without caring what's inside a page. Paging does support protection (per-page bits), segmentation isn't inherently faster, and segmentation's ideas persist broadly, not just in embedded systems.
